title: Percentage weight change: newborn weight loss and adult weight loss
blurb: Calculate percentage weight loss or gain and new weights for babies, children and adults.
question: A baby had a birth weight of 3500 g and weighs 3220 g on day 3. What percentage of the birth weight has been lost?

teach.h: Percentage change from the starting weight
teach.body: Formal rule: percentage lost = (original weight − new weight) ÷ original weight × 100. New weight after a known loss = original × (1 − percentage ÷ 100). Plain English: find the difference, compare it with where the person started, and turn that into a percentage. The midwifery practice paper used this for a newborn's birth weight.
teach.cite: FACTS.md section 4 (percentage change; Pearson midwifery practice paper)

steps.label: Same units
steps.sub: g with g, or kg with kg

teach.h: Worked example: baby Mia on day 3
teach.body: Mia was born weighing 3500 g and weighs 3220 g on day 3. Difference = 3500 − 3220 = 280 g. Percentage lost = 280 ÷ 3500 × 100 = 8%. Sense-check: 10% of 3500 g is 350 g, and 280 g is a little less, so a little under 10% fits.

teach.h: Worked example: Mr Okoro in clinic
teach.body: Mr Okoro weighed 92 kg and has lost 6% of his body weight. New weight = 92 × (1 − 0.06) = 92 × 0.94 = 86.48 kg, so 86.5 kg to one decimal place. The weight lost is 92 × 0.06 = 5.52 kg: that is not what the question asked for.

head: Starting weight
teach.caption: Estimate from 10% first; then calculate exactly.

teach.text: Dividing by the current weight instead of the original makes every loss look bigger (280 ÷ 3220 = 8.7%, not 8%). And when asked for the new weight, do not stop at the amount lost.

teach.body: Newborn weight loss is assessed against a percentage of birth weight; the figure comes from guidance and local policy, and a Part A stem will state it (the midwifery practice paper used a 10% loss on day 3). Use the stem's percentage: for a 3240 g baby, a 10% loss is 324 g, so the weight at that point is 2916 g.

items: Put both weights in the same unit first.
Divide by the original weight, never the current one.
Check whether the question wants the % lost, the amount lost or the new weight.

summary: You can now calculate a percentage weight change from the original weight and find a new weight after a stated percentage loss. You can also keep the units the same and avoid dividing by the current weight.

A.q: A baby had a birth weight of 3600 g and weighs 3330 g on day 3. What percentage of the birth weight has been lost? Write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Divided by the current weight instead of the birth weight.
whyNot.3: This is the percentage of birth weight remaining.

A.q: A child weighing 24 kg loses 5% of body weight during an illness. What does the child weigh now? Write your answer in kg to one decimal place.
A.why: New weight = 24 × 0.95 = 22.8 kg. Weight lost = 1.2 kg.

whyNot.1: This is the weight lost, not the new weight.

A.q: A man weighed 80 kg three months ago and now weighs 74.4 kg. What percentage of his body weight has he lost?

whyNot.1: Gave the kg lost, not the percentage.

B.q: A baby had a birth weight of 3240 g. The unit reviews any baby who has lost 10% of birth weight. What weight in grams represents a 10% loss?

whyNot.0: This is the amount lost, not the weight.

B.q: A baby had a birth weight of 3.8 kg and weighs 3.47 kg on day 4. What percentage of the birth weight has been lost? Write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: Multiplied the difference by 100 without dividing by the birth weight.

B.q: A woman weighing 68 kg loses 12% of her body weight during treatment. What does she weigh now? Write your answer in kg to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: This is the weight lost (8.16 kg).

C.q: A baby had a birth weight of 2.95 kg and weighs 2700 g on day 3. What percentage of the birth weight has been lost? Write your answer to one decimal place.
An infant weighing 9.4 kg loses 6.5% of body weight during an illness. What does the infant weigh now? Write your answer in kg to two decimal places.
A man weighed 72 kg before admission and now weighs 75.6 kg because of fluid retention. What is his percentage weight gain?

whyNot.0: Divided by the new weight instead of the original.
whyNot.2: Gave the kg gained, not the percentage.
whyNot.3: This is the new weight as a percentage of the original.

reteach.title: Always compare with the start
reteach.question: A baby born at 3400 g weighs 3150 g. What percentage has been lost?

blocks.body: Lost = 250 g. Compare it with the birth weight: 250 ÷ 3400 × 100 = 7.35%, so 7.4% to one decimal place. The birth weight is the reference point.

blocks.text: Using today's weight as the reference overstates the loss.

explain.body: Weight lost = original − new, in the same unit.

test.q: A baby had a birth weight of 3400 g and now weighs 3150 g. How much weight has been lost?

whyNot.0: Added the weights instead of subtracting.
whyNot.2: Place-value slip: the difference is 250 g.

test.q: A baby has lost 250 g from a birth weight of 3400 g. What percentage of the birth weight is this? Write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: Divided by the current weight (3150 g).

explain.body: New weight = original × (1 − % ÷ 100). A 5% loss means × 0.95.

test.q: A baby weighing 3.6 kg loses 5% of body weight. What does the baby weigh now? Write your answer in kg to two decimal places.

explain.body: Change kg to g (× 1000) or g to kg (÷ 1000) so both weights match.

test.q: A baby had a birth weight of 3.1 kg and now weighs 2900 g. What percentage of the birth weight has been lost? Write your answer to one decimal place.
